question: Define R(theta)=[[cos(theta/2),-sin(theta/2)],[sin(theta/2),cos(theta/2)]]. Derive the exact operator distance between R(a) and R(b), and prove it is at most |a-b|/2. Why does adding any number of untouched spectator qubits not multiply the distance by a dimension factor?
assumptions: Finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces unless real amplitudes are explicitly specified
All basis/register permutations are fixed and applied to both input and output
conventions: Column-vector action; Euclidean induced operator norm for norm claims
Source inspection only; no fresh formal verification
reference_answer:
All norms below are the Euclidean induced operator norm: ||M||=sup_(||v||=1)||Mv||, on the real plane or its complexification. Direct multiplication using cos^2(theta/2)+sin^2(theta/2)=1 shows R(theta)†R(theta)=I. Hence R(theta) is unitary (real orthogonal) and has operator norm one.

Put c=(a+b)/4 and h=(a-b)/4. The sum-difference identities give
cos(a/2)-cos(b/2)=-2 sin(c) sin(h),
sin(a/2)-sin(b/2)=2 cos(c) sin(h).
Keeping the minus sign of the upper-right entry, this gives
R(a)-R(b)=2 sin(h) [[-sin(c),-cos(c)],[cos(c),-sin(c)]]
=2 sin((a-b)/4) R((a+b)/2+pi).
This is exact matrix equality, including the sign of the real scalar; no phase has been discarded.

Norm homogeneity and the unitary norm-one identity therefore give
||R(a)-R(b)||=2|sin((a-b)/4)|.
Using |sin t|<=|t| proves ||R(a)-R(b)||<=|a-b|/2. The exact distance is always at most 2. In particular, equal angles give zero, a-b=4pi k gives zero for any integer k, and a-b=2pi(2k+1) gives distance 2. The last case differs by a minus sign as an exact matrix, which is not removed in this operator-distance convention.

For r>=0 untouched spectator qubits, the spectator space has dimension d=2^r>=1. In a tensor order with the target first, the difference is
(R(a)-R(b)) tensor I_d = 2 sin((a-b)/4) [R((a+b)/2+pi) tensor I_d].
The bracket is unitary, since its adjoint times itself is I_2 tensor I_d. Its induced operator norm is one on the nonzero tensor-product space; this argument applies to every input, including entangled target-spectator states. Thus the exact same distance holds after the lift. For a different fixed target-wire placement, both lifted gates are conjugated by the same basis-permutation unitary Q. Their difference is Q[(R(a)-R(b)) tensor I_d]Q†, and unitary conjugation preserves the induced norm, again giving the same value. There is no dimension multiplier because a unitary preserves vector length, whatever the dimension. One must not replace the induced norm by a sum of entry magnitudes or a Frobenius norm, which have different dimension behavior.

Zero spectators means d=1 and simply recovers the one-qubit result. A total register with zero qubits has no target wire on which this gate can act; it is not an additional distance-zero case. The result bounds exact matrix perturbation caused by changing a real angle; it does not compute rounded angles, synthesize gates over a discrete gate set, or certify finite-bit resource cost.

Partial credit for correct trigonometric differences or matrix products not fully assembled; do not require a particular proof route.

Uses the established matrix identity to obtain the exact distance 2|sin((a-b)/4)|, justifying equality rather than only an upper estimate. Accept orthogonality/unitarity and norm homogeneity, the Gram-matrix calculation, or a correct equivalent spectral/induced-norm argument.
Applies |sin t|<=|t| with the correct scaling to obtain |a-b|/2, retaining exact-vector/matrix phase conventions.

Proves spectator independence by a complete tensor-norm argument (including tensor unitarity, a Gram-matrix identity, or an equivalent induced-norm proof) and a common fixed unitary permutation/reindexing for wire placement. The argument covers all, including entangled, inputs; partial credit for a correct tensor proof without the fixed-placement explanation.

common_errors: Using 2|sin((a-b)/2)| and thereby losing the physical half-angle convention.
Dropping the sign of the scalar inside the exact factorization; absolute value belongs after taking the norm.
Using a Frobenius/entrywise dimension bound for the induced operator norm.
Checking only separable input vectors without a valid operator-norm argument for all joint states.
Treating a 2pi angle change as identical under an exact matrix metric, or reindexing the two compared gates differently.
Confusing zero spectators with zero total qubits and a nonexistent target wire.

boundary_cases.resolution: Exact distance two; the sign difference is retained.
Spectator space dimension one, so the one-qubit calculation is unchanged.
There is no target wire; not an active gate instance.
Covered because the scalar factor multiplies a unitary on the entire tensor space.

shared_results_produced.statement: For R(theta)=[[cos(theta/2),-sin(theta/2)],[sin(theta/2),cos(theta/2)]], ||R(a)-R(b)||=2|sin((a-b)/4)|<=|a-b|/2 in induced Euclidean operator norm. Tensoring both gates with any identity spectator space of positive finite dimension and applying the same fixed unitary basis permutation preserves this exact distance.

inputs.statement: a,b are real and R(theta) is the displayed half-angle matrix.
Norm means the Euclidean induced operator norm and exact matrices are compared.
There are r>=0 untouched spectator qubits, and the same fixed basis/wire placement is used for both gates.

steps.justification: Multiply the two-by-two matrices; use cos^2+sin^2=1 and cancellation of mixed terms.

assumptions: Same R convention for a and b.
steps.justification: Sum-difference identities produce entries [-sin c,-cos c;cos c,-sin c] with c=(a+b)/4.

assumptions: The rotation carrier has positive dimension.
steps.justification: A unitary preserves every vector norm and has induced norm one; scale by the absolute value of the signed scalar.

steps.claim: Lift the signed factorization to all spectators.
steps.conclusion: (R(a)-R(b)) tensor I_d is the same scalar times a joint unitary.
steps.justification: Tensor distribution preserves the difference and scalar, and (R tensor I_d)†(R tensor I_d)=I.

steps.claim: Place the gate on an arbitrary fixed physical wire.
assumptions: A common permutation Q is used for both compared gates.
steps.conclusion: The lifted physical distance equals 2|sin((a-b)/4)|, independent of d.
steps.justification: Conjugating the joint unitary by Q preserves unitarity; induced norm one applies to all joint vectors, not merely product inputs.

steps.claim: Transfer the same linear bound and diagnose endpoints.
assumptions: Exact phase convention and a valid target wire.
steps.conclusion: Spectator distance<=|a-b|/2; 4pi differences vanish, odd 2pi differences have distance 2; r=0 is allowed.
steps.justification: Substitute the sine values and note d=1 for zero spectators; a zero-total-qubit carrier has no gate target.
